Lassie enables doctors to focus on patients, not paperwork.

The average practice spends around 200 hours a month running itself. We have seen firsthand how the administrative burden is quietly breaking independent healthcare.

Most small businesses have something in common: they are run by reluctant operators. These are owners who set out to provide a service to their local community, and ended up running a business instead. They did not sign up to become finance people, HR people, recruiters, billers, or claims specialists. They became those things because someone had to.

Dental practices are a perfect example. Dentists go to school to practice dentistry and care for patients. Instead many are stuck doing paperwork, hiring people, training and retaining staff, negotiating insurance contracts, fighting claims, and managing cash flow.

Across roughly 160,000 dental practices in the U.S., this work is increasingly hard to staff and expensive to get wrong. AI can already do much of this work today. It is just not in the hands of these businesses yet.

We think businesses will soon run themselves, and small businesses will be among the first. Today, we are thrilled to announce that a16z is leading Lassie’s $35 million Series A – and partnering with a team solving exactly this problem.

Lassie is building AI that runs small businesses, starting with dental practices. Co-founders Steijn Pelle and Frédéric Renken did not find this problem from a distance. After working in consumer fintech at Robinhood and Coinbase, Steijn learned from his own dentist, Dr. Kwon, how complex the financial administration of an SMB dental practice can be. He and Frédéric, who had built product at Superhuman and Uber, then worked inside Dr. Kwon’s office, processing payments by hand to understand the workflow from the inside.

This story is emblematic of how Steijn and Frédéric have approached building Lassie. Before writing a single line of code, they spent months talking to dentists, primary care doctors, and healthcare finance teams. Then they spent years building the infrastructure and integrations required for agents to operate directly within a practice’s workflow: reading insurance claims, reconciling payments, posting to the ledger, and flagging claims that need action. Lassie is not a copilot that creates more work for the practice to review. It does the work.

Lassie already works with more than 700 practices across 49 states, generates more than $10 million in annualized revenue, and provides practices with 250,000 hours of labor a year. Growth has come largely through referrals and inbound demand – a sign that customers are not just buying the product, but telling other practice owners about it. The most important benefit, customers say, is not simply doing the work faster. It is catching the underpayments, denials, and missing claims that used to slip through.

Dental is a strong first market because the pain is acute and the workflows are structured, repetitive, and high-value. But the larger insight is not dental-specific. Every small business is still held together by human labor: people answer phones, schedule work, hire and train staff, chase paperwork, collect payments, reconcile accounts, follow up on exceptions, and keep the business moving. The last generation of software gave businesses better tools. AI agents change the unit of value from software to labor. Lassie is starting with dental, but the broader opportunity is much larger: the small business that runs itself.

That is also why Lassie is difficult to replicate with a generic model alone. Running a small business is not one task; it is thousands of recurring workflows across customers, vendors, payments, forms, systems, and exceptions. The product has to understand the business, connect to the tools where work happens, know when to act, and know when to ask. Over time, the product learns from every completed workflow, building a knowledge layer that is difficult to recreate from scratch.

We are thrilled to partner with Steijn, Frédéric, and the Lassie team as they build toward one of the most important shifts in software: from tools that help businesses operate to agents that do the work. If you know someone that owns a dental practice, check out the product here– and if you’re interested in joining the team, check out their open jobs here.

# GTM Associate

## Location

San Francisco, CA

## Employment Type

Full time

## Department

Sales

Our mission is to help small businesses run themselves. We’re starting with doctors’ offices, building autonomous systems that handle busywork and complete the workflows that keep the office moving every day. Our team is small, flat, and ambitious. We value craft, intellectual rigor, and direct communication.

# About the role

As a GTM Associate at Lassie, you'll create the first spark of demand. You'll identify promising doctors' offices, run thoughtful outreach you'd want to receive yourself, schedule demos, and help us learn which messages actually land with small businesses.

# What you'll do

- Build lists of promising doctors' offices and run thoughtful outreach across email, phone, social, events, and more
- Experiment with messages, segments, and channels to learn where demand is strongest
- Run early discovery conversations to understand who's working in the practice, how the office operates, and where Lassie may or may not fit
- Partner closely with Account Executives to schedule demos with offices that meet Lassie's ideal customer profile
- Keep the GTM engine organized, measured, and moving

- You have 1–2 years of SDR or BDR experience
- You move fast, think fast, and improve with every rep
- You never give up, with a smile on your face

- You're self-aware, flag what isn't working, and know how to improve
- You're excited about helping a small business run itself

# Joining us

Best Dental Billing PMS Integrations June 2026

If your dental practice management software integration only reads data from Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental but doesn't write payments back, you're still doing manual work. Someone has to open every EOB, match it to the claim, and post the payment by hand. For a typical practice, that manual reconciliation adds up to 80-100 hours every month. That's the difference between a dashboard that shows you information and dental billing software compatibility that actually closes the loop. A real integration posts insurance payments to the ledger automatically, matches deposits against your bank feed, and flags mismatches before they turn into AR problems. We'll compare which options run automatic posting across all three major PMS systems and which ones fall back to manual entry.

TLDR:

- PMS integrations eliminate manual EOB rekeying by automatically syncing payment data into Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental ledgers.
- Most competitors rely on humans for posting or cover only one PMS; few automate across all three major systems.
- Strong integrations write payments bidirectionally and match bank deposits against ledger lines in real time.
- Lassie automates posting across Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental with customizable rules and accuracy-first AI.

## What Are Practice Management Integrations for Dental Billing Software?

A practice management integration connects your dental billing software to the system of record where patient ledgers, claims, and production data live, namely Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental. When that link works, your billing tool reads appointment and claim data from the PMS and automatically writes payments, adjustments, and notes back to the ledger.

A solid integration handles core dental billing processes:

- Pulling claim and patient data from the PMS in real time
- Posting insurance payments and write-offs to the correct ledger line
- Matching deposits against bank activity
- Flagging mismatches before they age into AR

Integrations fall into two categories. Read-only integrations pull claim and patient data into your billing tool for visibility, but stop there. Bidirectional integrations go further: they automatically write payments, contractual adjustments, and write-offs back to the ledger, keeping the PMS current without manual entry.

The connection method matters for setup. Dentrix and Eaglesoft are typically installed on a local server, so integrations connect through a lightweight bridge application running on that server or via direct database access. Open Dental exposes a REST API, making cloud-based connections easier. Either way, the integration needs credentials, correct PMS version compatibility, and permission to write to the ledger, not just read from it.

Data flowing through a working integration includes ERA and EOB payment amounts, procedure codes, payer adjustments, patient responsibility splits, and deposit reference numbers for bank matching. Because this data includes protected health information, your billing software vendor should have a business associate agreement in place covering PMS access and payment processing. When that data writes back to the correct ledger line automatically, your AR reflects reality in real time rather than lagging days behind manual posting.

Without two-way sync, your front desk still rekeys every EOB by hand.

## How We Ranked the Best PMS Integration Options for Dental Billing

Our ranking leans on five criteria that separate workable integrations from cosmetic ones:

- Native support for Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental, three of the most widely used systems in US dental practices, per dental PMS market share data
- Depth of sync, meaning bidirectional writes back to the ledger versus read-only data pulls
- Automation level, from fully automatic posting to flag-and-review queues
- Setup complexity, including server requirements, API access, and onboarding time
- Reliability across PMS versions and cloud vs on-prem deployments

Rankings draw on vendor documentation, industry coverage, and verified user accounts, not hands-on internal testing.

## Best Overall PMS Integration for Dental Billing Software: Lassie

We built Lassie as AI-native software that posts EOBs directly into Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental. No exports, no scanning, no rekeying numbers off a PDF.

Core strengths

- Posting rules configured during onboarding to match each practice's adjustments, write-offs, and procedure-level logic
- Real-time bank reconciliation matches payer deposits to the PMS ledger lines down to the cent
- Accuracy-first architecture that flags ambiguous cases for review instead of guessing
- Centralized EOB storage with patient-name search for audits
- Multi-location support for practices sharing a PMS server across separate tax IDs
- Phased rollout by carrier, so you can validate posting against Delta Dental first
- Free EFT enrollment handled by our team to kill virtual credit card fees
- Automated secondary insurance claim filing for Open Dental practices, removing manual dual-insurance coordination

Max Shore - July 2, 2026

## Understanding Payment Posting in Open Dental

Payment posting records an insurance or patient payment against a specific claim or procedure inside your practice management system. In Open Dental, this happens through the Account module, where each payment attaches to a patient ledger, splits across procedures, and ties to a deposit batch that matches your bank statement.

Three layers matter here:

- Payments: the raw dollar amount received from a payer or patient.
- Splits: how that payment allocates across procedures, providers, and claim line items.
- Deposits: groupings of payments that match against actual bank deposits.

Open Dental treats unposted or misallocated payments as open AR, inflating aging reports and distorting provider production numbers.

## Manual Insurance Payment Posting Workflow

Here is the typical sequence a biller follows when posting an insurance check by hand in Open Dental:

1. Open the patient's Account module and locate the outstanding claim under the Insurance Claims grid.
2. Double click the claim, then choose "By Total" or "By Procedure" based on how the EOB itemizes payment.
3. Enter the check amount, check number, and date received in the Claim Payment window.
4. For each procedure, key in the insurance paid amount, write-off against the contracted fee, and any deductible.
5. Confirm the patient portion auto-calculates, then save the claim as received.
6. Attach the payment to a deposit slip under Manage > Deposit Slips.

Repeat for every claim on the EOB. A bulk check covering twelve patients means twelve separate windows and one shared deposit slip. Miss a write-off and the patient gets billed incorrectly. Skip the deposit slip and bank reconciliation breaks the next morning.

## Payment Splits and Allocation in Open Dental

Open Dental offers three allocation modes for splitting a payment across procedures, and the one you pick changes how strict the ledger math becomes.

### Split modes at a glance

| Mode | Behavior | When to use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Auto-split | Distributes payment across oldest charges first | High-volume practices that trust aging order |
| Manual split | Biller assigns each dollar to a specific procedure | Complex EOBs with downgrades or denials |
| Rigorous accounting | Forces every payment to attach to a procedure | Multi-provider practices needing clean production reports |

Rigorous mode, set under Setup > Account > Account Preferences, prevents floating credits and keeps provider production numbers accurate.

Manual review is required when an EOB downgrades a procedure, applies a deductible to one line, or denies one procedure while paying others. Auto-split cannot read EOB reason codes. See the Open Dental payment documentation for each mode.

## Insurance EOB Reconciliation Best Practices

Reconciliation is the daily checkpoint that catches what posting missed. Treat it as a three-way match: the EOB, the entry in Open Dental, and the bank deposit need to agree to the cent before you close the day.

A reliable daily rhythm looks like this:

- Pull the Daily Payments report under Reports > Standard > Daily and filter by payment type.
- Cross-reference each posted insurance payment against the EOB total, including interest or capitation amounts.
- Confirm the deposit slip total matches the EFT or check batch hitting your bank account.
- Investigate unallocated income before it ages into the next billing cycle.

Monthly, pair the Insurance Aging report with your bank statement to catch EFTs without EOBs, payer takebacks posted as negative adjustments, and bundled payments spanning multiple deposit dates. The Zeldent reconciliation tips guide covers edge cases worth knowing.

## Common Payment Posting Errors and How to Avoid Them

The same handful of mistakes show up across most practices we audit. Each one looks small in isolation and compounds into AR drag over a quarter.

- Write-off math that ignores the contracted fee: posting the billed amount as paid inflates patient balances and triggers refund requests later.
- Misapplied patient responsibility: keying the deductible into the wrong procedure line creates statement disputes.
- Unfinalized batch payments: leaving a Claim Payment window saved but not marked received holds the claim open and skews aging.
- EOB versus deposit date mismatches: breaks the daily three-way match.
- Downgrades posted as paid: buries an appeal opportunity.

Prevention comes down to two habits: configure fee schedules so write-offs auto-calculate, and route any line with a reason code through a second reviewer before saving.

## Electronic Remittance Advice (ERA) and Auto-Posting in Open Dental

ERAs (the 835 file format) are the digital twin of a paper EOB. Once enrolled with a payer, the file lands under Manage > Claims ERAs and auto-populates check amount, paid-by-procedure breakdowns, write-offs, and CARC reason codes against matching claims.

Setup requires three pieces:

- Activating Setup > Family/Insurance > Insurance Payment Setup so ERAs route to the correct provider.
- Matching the EFT trace number to the bank deposit before finalizing the batch.

The Open Dental ERA 835 manual covers payer-specific quirks. The catch: ERAs only cover enrolled payers, and smaller carriers still send paper PDFs that demand manual entry.

## Configuring EFT Payments and Bank Reconciliation

EFT enrollment moves insurance payments from paper checks into direct bank deposits, usually settling in two to three business days instead of two weeks. Each payer has its own enrollment portal, voided check requirement, and W-9 step.

A workable setup sequence:

- Enroll payer by payer through the carrier's provider portal or your clearinghouse's EFT service.
- Capture the EFT trace number (TRN segment in the 835) for every deposit and store it against the matching ERA in Open Dental.
- Match the trace number to the bank ledger line before finalizing the deposit slip under Manage > Deposit Slips.

## Batch Insurance Payment Processing in Open Dental

When one check or EFT pays ten or more claims, posting each through the single-claim workflow wastes time. Open Dental's Manage > Batch Insurance window records the deposit once and attaches every claim to it.

The workflow:

# Ex-Robinhood and Superhuman alums raise $35M in a16z-led round to let AI run small businesses end-to-end

June 4, 2026

4 minute read

Image credits: Lassie

- Lassie has raised $35 million in a Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz, bringing its total funding to $47 million.
- Co-founders Steijn Pelle and Frédéric Renken spent months working inside a dental practice by hand before writing a single line of code.
- The company now operates in 700+ practices across 49 states and saves owners over 250,000 hours of administrative work each year.

When Steijn Pelle’s dentist showed him what it actually takes to run a dental practice, he didn’t go back to his laptop and start building. He pulled up a bar stool in the back office and spent months processing insurance claims and reconciling payments by hand. That experience — working inside Dr. Kwon’s Bay Area practice — shaped every product decision that followed at Lassie.

San Francisco-based Lassie announced it has raised $35 million in Series A financing, bringing its total capital raised to $47 million. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, which closed a $15 billion mega-fund in January 2026 with a stated thesis of backing AI companies that replace operational drag. The round also drew support from Night Capital, Rahul Vohra (founder and former CEO of Superhuman), Zach Perret (co-founder and CEO of Plaid, valued at $8 billion in its most recent secondary), Taavet Hinrikus (co-founder and former CEO of Wise), Gokul Rajaram, and Brian Balfour (co-founder and CEO of Reforge).

Alex Rampell, co-founder of Affirm and General Partner at a16z, is joining Lassie’s board. Dr. Ed Zuckerberg and Jason Warnick, former CFO of Robinhood, join as advisors.

Lassie was founded by Steijn Pelle, an early product manager at Robinhood and Coinbase, and Frédéric Renken, the first product hire at Superhuman. Previous backers include SV Angel, Homebrew, and Go Global Ventures.

## The $200,000 problem

A typical doctor’s office loses more than 100 hours a month to administrative work and spends roughly $200,000 a year on staff that owners can barely find, let alone keep. Lassie’s agent goes directly into a practice’s insurance portals, pulls reimbursements, reconciles them against records, updates the system of record, and verifies funds in the bank — replacing human labour entirely rather than adding another layer of software on top of it.

The company operates in more than 700 practices across 49 states and currently provides business owners with over 250,000 hours of labour each year. It is part of a broader wave of agentic AI companies— such as octonomy, which raised $20M to automate complex enterprise workflows — that are moving the market from AI tools that assist to AI systems that execute.

“Small business owners should be freed up from doing busywork, so they can focus on what they are passionate about. After watching 700 businesses rely on Lassie to do a big part of their administration, I am convinced that the future is bright.” — Steijn Pelle, CEO and co-founder.

“I am thrilled to partner with Steijn, Frédéric, and the team as they build towards one of the most important shifts in software: from tools that help businesses operate to agents that do the work.” — Alex Rampell, General Partner, a16z.

“Before Lassie, I was drowning in paperwork. Now, Lassie saves us over 100 hours a month and payments that used to take four to five weeks hit our account in less than a week.” — Dr. Eric Kwon, founder, Grace Dental.

## The competitive landscape

Lassie competes with deeply entrenched legacy systems. Dentrix, owned by Henry Schein and trusted by more than 35,000 practices, offers a broad suite covering scheduling, billing, imaging, and analytics but requires staff to operate it. NexHealth focuses on patient communication and intake automation but does not autonomously execute financial back-office tasks. The broader race to build AI that does work rather than advises has attracted significant capital — Decagon raised $250M at a $4.5B valuation on a similar premise in enterprise customer service. Where these platforms give practices better tools, Lassie’s bet is that practices want the work done for them entirely.

a16z has backed this thesis before: Pit, a Stockholm-based startup building custom AI systems to replace manual enterprise workflows, secured $16M from the firm in May 2026 — with the same Alex Rampell on record saying “every company can now run on systems they actually designed themselves.”

## Market context

According to Grand View Research, the global AI automation market was valued at $129.92 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $1.14 trillion by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 31.4% — with healthcare expected to be the fastest-growing vertical at 36% annually.

The real question Lassie forces the market to answer is not whether AI can handle dental paperwork. It already does. The harder question is how far autonomous back-office systems can expand before practice owners start asking what, exactly, they still need staff for.

# How Steijn Pelle built Lassie to help small businesses run themselves using AI

### 800+ small businesses across the country are using Lassie to run themselves, and Steijn just raised another $35M to take Lassie to the next level

Katie Kirsch and Cola Gahm

Aug 24, 2026

13

1

2

Share

AI is getting rapidly adopted by Fortune 500 companies and law firms… but what about the millions of small businesses that keep the world running, like your local doctor, plumber, or auto-mechanic?

It turns out, small businesses are more eager to adopt AI than you might think. In fact, hundreds of businesses across the US are now already partly running themselves using AI - including managing paperwork, updating their systems, and soon, interacting and transacting with customers - thanks to Lassie.

Lassie is building the autonomous systems that take care of all the busywork behind running a small business - so that owners can finally focus on what they do best (their craft) and get their time back.

Since founding the company a few years ago, Steijn Pelle has scaled Lassie to 800+ small businesses across 49 states, starting with doctors’ offices. A few months ago, he raised a $35M Series A led by a16z, bringing the company’s total funding to $47M. Now, he’s on a mission to scale Lassie - and create a future world where every small business runs itself, using AI.

---

steijnpelle@steijnpelleToday, we're introducing Lassie and $47M in funding led by a16z. We're building AI that runs small businesses, starting with doctors' offices. Lassie is already trusted by 700+ practices across the country, working autonomously to provide them with 30 hours of labor per month. 2:49 PM · Jun 3, 2026 · 1.19M Views203 Replies · 151 Reposts · 2.91K Likes

---

### The founding story

Before founding Lassie, Steijn was one of the first product managers at both Robinhood and Coinbase - and always had a passion for solving hard problems with technology.

The idea for Lassie came out of a conversation he had with his own doctor, Dr. Kwon, in Menlo Park, CA. Dr. Kwon shared with Steijn that the most challenging part of running his own business wasn’t the craft - it was the 200+ hours per month that he and his team spent on paperwork.

All the tedious, manual, detail-oriented work that they struggled to find staff members to do, and that Dr. Kwon was forced to do himself after-hours - like managing insurance payments, catching underpaid claims, appealing denials, and going back and forth with patients on bills and appointments.

Steijn could sense that there was a huge business opportunity here. Millions of small businesses each spend tens (if not hundreds) of thousands of dollars per year on the kind of busywork that Dr. Kwon was describing.

From left to right: Frédéric Renken, Dr. Kwon, and Steijn Pelle

Steijn also knew it could take years of unglamorous work to fully understand the busywork required to run small businesses - let alone, build a solution that would autonomously run it for business owners in a way that complied with a complex, manual, and highly-regulated industry.

Most founders would have looked right past this space (what Paul Graham calls, “ schlep blindness”) or given up. But for that rare founder with the patience and grit to figure things out from first principles - the reward would be enormous.

This was an opportunity to capture an underserved market that was desperate for a solution to automate the thousands of uninteresting, overlooked tasks that bottleneck small businesses every single day, on a recurring basis.

“AI that autonomously runs small businesses” is what Lassie’s new board member Alex Rampell would call a“Goldilocks zone” - a market that’s not the main priority for frontier AI labs to own themselves, and too messy for a generic model to serve, but big enough to matter.

Maybe it was the competitive runner in him - or that he had seen enough close friends train for years and compete in the Olympics - but Steijn wasn’t afraid of playing the long game. In fact, it was exactly the challenge he had been looking for.

---

### Bringing Lassie to life

You have to learn how to walk before you can run. For Steijn and his team, that meant - you have to learn how to run a small business yourself, before you can train AI to do it for you. So, Steijn and his team signed up to take on all the paperwork for two different doctors’ offices - Dr. Kwon’s in Menlo Park, and a gastroenterologist’s in Scranton. And they didn’t just do this for a few days, then quit - they did this manual work for a year.

To give an example day in the life, Steijn would comb through hundreds of payments from an insurance portal, enter them into the practice management system one by one, print a forty-page list of patients who needed a bill, and finish the day checking everyone’s balances and generating statements. Steijn smiles while thinking about those days: “I felt like Jim Halpert from The Office!”

Co-founders Frédéric Renken (left) and Steijn Pelle (right)

After he and his team figured out the jobs to be done, they started training autonomous systems to do the work for them. Given that they were operating in such a hands-on, heavily-regulated space, handling sensitive financial and personal health information (PHI) - there was no room for error. Lassie didn’t just have to be good, it had to be correct. It took several more years for the product to be ready to scale.

One of the things that had impressed Steijn most at Robinhood was how relentlessly the team worked to seamlessly onboard new users - with little to no manual account approval. Similarly at Superhuman, where his co-founder Frédéric Renken was the first product hire, the team had obsessed over removing friction at the critical moment when people first touch the product.

To learn how to sell and deploy AI at scale, Steijn and his team started by taking the non-scalable approach: first, doing it all in-person. They spent more than a year traveling around the country to visit small business owners, sit with them at their computers, and personally install Lassie onto their systems. Through this, Steijn and his team built a winning playbook for codifying the sale and productizing the implementation of Lassie at scale. Along the way, they also converted their first 100 earliest adopters into some of the biggest champions for the company.

Dr. Kwon is one of those proud early adopters of Lassie - now able to see almost twice as many patients and still make it home in time for dinner with his family. Many customers like him are clinking champagne to celebrate the time Lassie is saving them. Someone recently told Steijn that Lassie “saved his marriage.”

---

### Building the culture and team that scales

A lot has changed since Steijn’s earliest days of building Lassie, but some things haven’t. His approach to operating at the lowest level of detail first, doing things with rigor of thought, and valuing the craft of building something wonderful- is clearly deeply rooted into the company’s culture.

The team is all in. 15 people, in-person in San Francisco, sprinting to make Lassie the AI company that makes entrepreneurship easier for all small businesses. In their first 90 days at the company, every new team member spends time working in a few real small businesses, just like Steijn and Frédéric once did - so they know what it’s like to schlep (err, step) in small business owners’ shoes.

When asked about the most important team values at Lassie, Steijn is quick to answer - the Lassie team doesn’t ship junk, likes rigor of thought, and cares about direct communication.

Steijn is planning to triple the Lassie team in the next year - and he’s about to open a brand-new office in Jackson Square, complete with an open kitchen, beautiful Scandinavian-style co-working spaces, and an in-house chef who previously worked for the Collison brothers.

A glimpse into Lassie’s new San Francisco office

Ultimately, Steijn is in this for the long haul - a marathon of sprints, if you will - and he’s looking for people who are just as persistent and passionate about solving hard problems. If that sounds like you, come build Lassie with him.

---

### Open Roles

Lassie is hiring across the board. A few open roles that stand out:

Deployment Strategist- Be on the frontlines of getting AI deployed to small businesses. And with that build the playbooks for implementation, account management, and maintain the bar for turning customers into fans. Together with the people that did this for Superhuman and Robinhood.

Head of Marketing- Build Lassie’s growth marketing engine that helps to make millions of small business owners aware that AI can now help them run their business.

Product Engineer- Build the products small businesses use every day to get work done without adding more work to manage.

Head of Finance- As Lassie’s first finance hire, you’ll build the AI-native financial operations from scratch alongside CEO Steijn Pelle and advisor Jason Warnick (former CFO, Robinhood) - owning everything from monthly close, strategic finance projects like pricing, and building the operating model, to supporting future fundraises.

Founding Recruiter- Help recruit a world-class team that can bring AI to millions of small businesses across the world.

# Lassie Raises $35M Series A To Make Dental Practices Run Themselves

Andreessen Horowitz leads a $35 million Series A in Lassie, an AI agent platform now running back-office work for 700+ dental practices across 49 U.S. states with $10M ARR.

Kaan Tınmaz Jun 5, 2026 Updated Jul 12, 2026

Andreessen Horowitz is leading a $35 million Series A in Lassie, a San Francisco startup building autonomous AI agents that take over the financial back office of small businesses, beginning with dental practices. The round announced on June 3, 2026 brings Lassie's total funding to $47 million and signals that vertical AI agents are becoming a credible substitute for the manual labor that keeps small enterprises afloat.

## From Robinhood And Superhuman To Dental Ledgers

Lassie was founded in 2025 by Steijn Pelle, formerly of Robinhood and Coinbase, and Frederic Renken, who built product at Superhuman and Uber. The pair spent months inside a Bay Area dental practice run by Dr. Kwon, posting payments by hand to understand how claims, reimbursements and ledgers actually move. That field work shaped a product that does not ask dentists to write prompts. Lassie reads insurance claims, reconciles payments, posts to the ledger and flags denials that need follow up, replacing tasks usually done by a billing specialist.

## Traction That Convinced a16z

The company already works with more than 700 practices across 49 states, generates more than $10 million in annualized revenue and says it returns roughly 250,000 hours of labor a year to its customers. Growth has come largely through referrals from practice owners. a16z general partner Alex Rampell and partner Olivia Moore wrote in their investment note that the largest gain Lassie delivers is not speed but catching the underpayments, denials and missing claims that previously slipped through.

## The Vertical AI Agent Playbook

Lassie is part of a wave of vertical AI startups raising fresh capital in early June 2026. The same day, a16z also announced a $55 million Series A in personal assistant company Town. The thesis is identical to deals like Town's a16z and Forerunner round and earlier bets including Mecka AI's $60M Series A: AI changes the unit of value from software to labor, and the businesses that pay for labor are huge. The U.S. has roughly 160,000 dental practices alone. Pelle and Renken say they will extend Lassie next into primary care offices and other owner-operated medical services, where the workflow patterns of insurance claims and patient billing rhyme with dentistry.

The round adds to a busy week for AI funding that also included Generalist AI's $400M raise at a $2B valuation and a flurry of agent platform deals tied to Microsoft's MAI model family unveiled at Build 2026.

# 6 Best Dental Software Programs in June 2026

Compare the 6 best dental software programs in June 2026. See which tools automate EOB posting, reconciliation, and claims for Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental.

Max Shore - July 6, 2026

You probably chose Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental years ago, and switching your entire practice management system just to get better insurance posting sounds like overkill. That's where standalone dental software programs come in: they sit on top of your existing PMS and automate the revenue cycle tasks that eat up staff hours, like posting EOBs, matching deposits, and filing secondary claims.

The catch is that the options have real limits. Zentist automates posting for Open Dental only, while eAssist and DayDream still route the work through human billers instead of true software automation.

We ranked six options by PMS coverage, posting accuracy, implementation speed, and whether the product actually does the work or outsources it to a team.

TLDR:

- Dental software automates insurance posting, reconciliation, and claims to cut manual work hours
- Key split: AI tools post automatically while billing agencies route work through human staff
- Zentist automates posting for Open Dental only; eAssist and DayDream use human billers
- Curve is a full practice management system replacement, not a revenue cycle add-on
- Lassie automates EOB posting across Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental without human billers

## What Are Dental Software Programs?

Dental software programs are the tools practices use to handle the financial mechanics of running an office: filing insurance claims, posting payments, matching EOBs against bank deposits, chasing unpaid balances, and tracking accounts receivable. Some come built into practice management systems like Dentrix, Eaglesoft, or Open Dental. Others sit on top of those systems to automate specific revenue cycle tasks.

The category splits along one line that matters more than feature lists: who actually does the work. On one side are billing agencies and tech-enabled services, where human billers log into a dashboard and post payments by hand, the same labor model whether the team sits in-house, offshore, or behind a software front end. On the other side is AI-native software that retrieves, reads, and posts EOBs directly into the PMS with no human in the loop. The distinction drives everything downstream: accuracy down to the cent, how fast a practice gets paid, whether the tool scales without adding headcount, and whether it carries the turnover and embezzlement risk that comes with manual posting teams.

The category exists because dental billing is paperwork-heavy and error-prone. Practices still receive paper checks and EOBs from payers, key payments into the PMS by hand, then match those entries against bank deposits across dozens of payers, while denials, downgrades, and adjustments pile up unworked.

That manual cycle consumes a large share of a practice's administrative hours each month and routinely leaves reimbursements waiting 30-plus days. According to a 2025 ADA Health Policy Institute poll, more than half of dentists surveyed cited insurance-related issues, including delayed or denied payments, as a top concern heading into 2026.

According to industry analysis, the average dental practice loses between 10 to 15 percent of its annual revenue to billing inefficiencies, including uncollected balances, aging AR, avoidable claim denials, and verification errors, and in 2026, payers are tightening documentation requirements, making this harder to ignore.

The right software shrinks that workload, gets practices paid faster, catches posting errors before they reach the ledger, and keeps AR from piling up while clinicians focus on patient care.

## How We Ranked Dental Software Programs

We looked at each product against a consistent set of criteria, drawing from publicly available product pages, demos, and customer-facing positioning.

- Automation depth: does the software actually do the posting work, or does a human team behind a dashboard do it?
- PMS coverage: support for Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental, since these are the three systems most independent practices run on.
- Posting and reconciliation accuracy: how the product handles edge cases, adjustments, and bank-to-PMS matching.
- Implementation speed: how quickly a practice can go live without disrupting daily work.
- Pricing transparency: whether fees are published or hidden behind sales calls.
- Scalability: whether the product holds up across multi-location groups and growing claim volume.

Lassie is the only fully AI-native dental software that automates EOB posting across Dentrix, Eaglesoft, and Open Dental without human billers behind the scenes. We retrieve, read, and post insurance payments directly into your PMS with customizable rules, real time bank reconciliation, and accuracy down to the cent.

- Automated EOB posting with customizable adjustment rules configured during onboarding
- Real time banking reconciliation across insurance payments and deposits
- Multi location support with separate financial tracking by practice
- Automated secondary insurance claim filing for dual coverage patients

Bottom line: Lassie replaces manual insurance posting with pure software, giving practices embezzlement proof accuracy, round the clock availability, and an average four to seven percent revenue lift without the headcount risk of human billing agencies.

## Zentist

Zentist offers cloud-based insurance revenue cycle management with Remit AI, which automates EOB and ERA data intelligence and matches against bank transactions from a wide range of dental payers. Its recent payment posting automation runs on the Open Dental API, targeting DSOs and multi location groups.

What They Offer

- Automated retrieval of insurance payments by logging into payer portals and parsing EOB and ERA data
- Dashboard tracking outstanding claims until processed
- Faster payment posting for practices on the automation, per Zentist's product positioning
- DentalXChange clearinghouse integration for expanded payer connectivity

Good for: DSOs on Open Dental wanting RCM analytics across operations.

Limitation: Posting automation works only on Open Dental. Dentrix and Eaglesoft practices still depend on human billers.

Bottom line: Zentist fits Open Dental DSOs needing enterprise RCM dashboards, while Lassie covers full AI posting across all three major PMS systems.

## eAssist Dental Solutions

eAssist is an outsourced dental billing and insurance claims service where specialists use the company's portal to handle claims work for practices. The company describes itself as a large outsourced dental billing provider, assigning each office a dedicated remote team.

What They Offer

- Billing experts pursuing every dollar in over 90 day uncollected insurance aging until reaching zero balance
- Proprietary software, invoicing services, IT, and HIPAA compliance support
- Remote work model with human billing specialists working from home
- A dedicated remote team assigned to each office, with the same billers working that account instead of a rotating pool

Good for: Practices wanting a full service agency for revenue cycle outsourcing, complex claims, and appeals with humans in the loop.

Limitation: Human billers still post manually, carrying risks of typos, turnover, and embezzlement common to labor based models.

## DayDream Dental

DayDream is a tech-powered dental billing company that manages insurance accounts receivable by submitting clean claims, posting payments, appealing denials, and tracking claim status. AI agents layer on top of a billing agency workflow covering verification, claims, and reconciliation.

What They Offer

- Insurance verification ahead of appointments, with coverage details and fee schedules pushed back into the PMS
- AI powered revenue cycle management for claims follow up
- AI agents that chase errant claims in weeks instead of years

Good for: Practices wanting a full service billing partner that pairs AI agents with human billers.

Limitation: DayDream is still a billing agency at its core, so practices keep the staffing risks of agency models. Many claim denials are potentially avoidable, caused by data entry errors and missing information that human billers introduce during manual posting.

Bottom line: DayDream fits offices that want humans in the loop with automation layered on. Lassie delivers posting and reconciliation as pure software, without agency dependencies.

## Curve Dental

Curve Dental is a cloud based practice management software handling charting, treatment planning, scheduling, and billing in one system. It targets dental teams wanting anywhere access without managing on premise servers.

What They Offer

- Billing tools covering invoicing, click to pay options, payment posting, and eClaims submission and tracking
- EFT auto posting that matches insurance payments with remittance details and routes them to the correct patient and procedure
- All in one practice management, imaging, and patient engagement software for practices of any size

Good for: Offices wanting an all in one cloud PMS that consolidates scheduling, clinical notes, imaging, and billing.

Limitation: Curve is a full PMS replacement, lacking the granular custom rules and AI reconciliation of dedicated revenue cycle tools.

Bottom line: Curve suits offices ready to swap their entire PMS. Lassie works with your existing PMS.

## Location

San Francisco, CA

Full time

Engineering

Our mission is to help small businesses run themselves. We’re starting with doctors’ offices, building autonomous systems that handle busywork and complete the workflows that keep the office moving every day. Our team is small, flat, and ambitious. Data pipelines processing $1B+ in insurance claims

Python (Django, Pydantic AI), Postgres, Redis

Google Cloud Platform, Vercel

Linear, Slack, Notion

_request.systemPrompt:
You are a senior B2B account researcher producing a decision-grade dossier on ONE exact
company for a sales team that sells an AI account-based-marketing platform.

THE EXACT TARGET, and nothing else:
  Company: Lassie
  Domain: www.lassie.ai (the marketing site also resolves at getlassie.com)
  LinkedIn: linkedin.com/company/lassie
  What it is: a San Francisco AI startup building "AI that runs the doctor's office" - automating
  administrative and insurance/billing workflows for independent dental and medical practices.
  Founders: Steijn Pelle and Frederic (Frederik) Renken. Raised a $35M Series A led by Andreessen
  Horowitz, announced 3 June 2026.

DISAMBIGUATION - THIS IS CRITICAL. Several unrelated entities share the name "Lassie":
  - Lassie (lassie.co / lassie.se), a Swedish/European PET INSURANCE company - NOT the target.
  - Lassie, the fictional collie / the film and TV franchise - NOT the target.
  - Any veterinary, pet-care, or dog-related "Lassie" - NOT the target.
If a source is about pet insurance, pets, dogs, or the TV collie, DISCARD it and say so. Only use
sources that are unambiguously about the SF dental/healthcare-admin AI company at lassie.ai.

Ground EVERY fact in a public page. For every fact give: the fact, a VERBATIM QUOTE copied exactly
from the source, and the SOURCE URL. If a fact cannot be found on a public page, write
"NOT FOUND" - never guess, never infer a number, never fill a gap with a plausible-sounding claim.
Prefer primary sources (lassie.ai pages, the company's own job postings on jobs.ashbyhq.com/lassie,
the a16z announcement, the BusinessWire release, founder posts) over aggregators.

Write a long, dense, well-organised markdown report with these numbered sections. Do not skip a
section; if a section has nothing, write the heading and "NOT FOUND".

1. IDENTITY AND DISAMBIGUATION - legal/operating name, HQ, founding year, what it actually sells,
   in one paragraph; then an explicit list of same-name entities you EXCLUDED and why.
2. PRODUCT AND TARGET VERTICAL - exactly what the product does, which practice types it serves
   (dental? medical? veterinary?), which workflows it automates (claims, EOB, insurance
   verification, phone, scheduling), pricing if public, integrations/PMS or EHR systems named.
   Quote the product pages.
3. CUSTOMERS AND TRACTION - number of practices/dentists served, named customers, ARR or revenue
   claims, growth claims, testimonials. Quote each.
4. FUNDING HISTORY - every round with date, amount, stage, lead investor, participating investors,
   and the announcement URL. Include any seed/pre-seed round before the Series A.
5. TEAM AND GTM COMPOSITION - total headcount, engineering vs sales vs marketing split, and
   specifically: do they have ANY dedicated salespeople, marketers or SDRs today? Name every
   employee you can find with their title (LinkedIn, team page, job postings, press).
6. GO-TO-MARKET MOTION - hard evidence of HOW they acquire customers: founder-led selling,
   in-person events/study clubs, referrals, outbound email/cold calling, paid ads, direct mail,
   conferences/trade shows, partnerships with DSOs or dental service organizations. Quote the
   evidence. Also: any public evidence of the sales/marketing TOOLS they use (CRM, outbound
   tooling, ad platforms).
7. HIRING SIGNALS - every open role you can find, especially go-to-market roles (growth, GTM,
   account executive, SDR, marketing). For each: exact title, location, posting URL, and a
   verbatim quote from the job description describing the go-to-market work. Note salary bands
   if published.
8. LEADERSHIP AND KEY PEOPLE - the founders and any executives/leads, with exact titles, prior
   companies, and a source URL each. Flag who appears to own revenue/growth.
9. OPERATIONAL PAIN AND STRATEGIC MOVES - what problems the company itself is publicly wrestling
   with (scaling sales into a fragmented SMB market, hiring, distribution), and its stated
   strategy/roadmap (new verticals beyond dental, new products). Quote statements from founders
   or investors.
10. CULTURE AND RESONANCE - how the company writes and talks about itself: values, tone, working
    style, what founders say publicly, employee sentiment if any exists, any publicly aired
    frustrations. Quote the exact language.
11. TIMING SIGNALS - dated events in the last ~18 months (funding, launches, hires, expansions,
    press) with dates and URLs, newest first.
12. SOURCE LIST - every URL you used, one per line, each marked [primary] or [secondary].
